question: Which statement best describes Stack vs heap?
options: Primitive values (numbers, booleans, small fixed-size data) and references live on the call stack, which is fast and automatically unwound when a function returns. Objects, arrays, and functions live on the heap, a larger pool of memory that the garbage collector manages. A variable holding an object actually holds a reference (a pointer) on the stack to the object's location on the heap.

Modern engines use a mark-and-sweep algorithm. Starting from the roots, the collector marks every value it can reach by traversing references. In the sweep phase it frees everything that was not marked. Because it works from reachability rather than reference counts, mark-and-sweep correctly collects cycles (objects that reference each other but are unreachable from any root).

A value is reachable if it can be accessed from a root (the global object, the current call stack, and active closures) by following references. Reachable values are kept; unreachable values become eligible for collection. The entire model rests on this single idea: memory is freed not when you stop using a value, but when nothing can reach it anymore.

Memory is allocated implicitly whenever you create a value: declaring a variable, building an object or array literal, defining a function, or concatenating strings. You never call malloc; the engine reserves space as values come into existence. Knowing where allocation happens helps you reason about what the collector will later need to free.

question: Which statement best describes Allocation?
options: An older strategy counts how many references point to each object and frees it when the count hits zero. It is simple but fails on cyclic references: two objects that point at each other keep each other's count above zero forever, even when nothing else can reach them. This is exactly why engines moved to reachability-based mark-and-sweep.

Even with automatic GC, code can keep values reachable longer than intended. The classic culprits are: accidental globals, timers (setInterval) that are never cleared, closures that retain large objects, detached DOM nodes still referenced in JS, and event listeners that are never removed. Each keeps a reference alive that prevents collection.

WeakMap, WeakSet, and WeakRef hold references that do NOT prevent garbage collection. If the only remaining reference to an object is weak, the collector may reclaim it.
